caption:
Which of these 7 Kyoto secrets didn't you know? Comment the number 👇

1. Fushimi Inari Shrine
Fushimi Inari's famous orange tunnel is built from more than 10,000 torii gates, each one donated by a person or company. The donor's name and the date of the gift are carved into the back of every gate.

2. Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion)
In 1950, a 22-year-old novice monk burned Kinkaku-ji to the ground, destroying a building more than 500 years old. It was rebuilt in 1955 as a close copy of the original, and its top two floors are covered in real gold leaf.

3. Kiyomizu-dera
Kiyomizu-dera's wooden stage stands 13 meters above the hillside, held up by interlocking joints with no nails. In the Edo period, people jumped off it believing that surviving would grant a wish. Temple records count 234 jumps, and about 85% of the jumpers survived.

4. Nijo Castle
The corridors of Nijo Castle's Ninomaru Palace have "nightingale floors" that chirp with every step. Legend says they were an alarm so no ninja could sneak up on the shogun. The castle's own sign says the sound comes from nails rubbing against metal clamps as the boards wore over the centuries.

5. Ginkaku-ji (Silver Pavilion)
Despite its name, a 2007 survey found no trace of silver on Ginkaku-ji. Whether the shogun who built it ran out of money or never planned any, its wooden exterior has stayed bare for over 500 years.

6. Arashiyama Bamboo Grove
The wind moving through Arashiyama's towering bamboo is one of Japan's "100 Soundscapes", a list the government drew up of everyday sounds worth noticing and preserving.

7. Gion
Gion's traditional ochaya teahouses still follow ichigensan okotowari, "no first-timers": without a personal introduction from an existing client, no amount of money will get you a seat.
